text: A flaming rock lands in the hills and the townspeople walk out to look at it, as though a carnival had come. Byron Haskin keeps a newsreel tempo after that: sightseers, then sirens, then a military line drawn on a map, then the same line redrawn further back. Eighty-five minutes leaves no room for deliberation, and the film spends none. Its one large idea is stated flatly and then kept - the invaders are not merely better armed than what is sent against them but unbothered by it, and even the atomic bomb is filed among the things that will be tried. The Academy's award for special effects went to work that still holds without allowance made: the Martian craft do not stomp or roar, they drift sideways, slow and level, and the hills underneath them stop looking solid.

A gas company sends a man to buy the right to drill under other people's fields, and he is good at the job. The work is persuasion, done one signature at a time, and Gus Van Sant attends to that transaction rather than to any rig: what a per-acre figure sounds like said out loud to the person who farms the acre. The salesman believes a fair amount of what he says. That is the film's difficulty as well as its subject, because a man convinced he is doing a town a favour cannot be beaten the way a villain can. A hundred and six minutes, largely conversation, the argument moving through people who will have to keep living next to each other afterward. The National Board of Review put it among its ten of 2012, which for a drama built out of meetings and small print is a fair reading.

Ships are going down and no one can say why; then the cause turns out to have a captain. Richard Fleischer spends a good part of his 127 minutes on that shift, from maritime rumour to the interior of a machine, and once the investigators are aboard the Nautilus the adventure becomes a matter of hospitality with no exit. Nemo answers to no navy. Critics have since read the film beside the decade's other stories about one man in possession of a force no nation can match, and the reading fits: he has built the thing, he uses it as he pleases, and he receives his guests courteously while making it plain they will not be leaving. The Academy's award for colour art direction accounts for the rest - brass, rivets, deep upholstery, an organ, portholes onto water lit like weather.

The scheme belongs to a daughter: she picks a woman out for her father, a woman whose own marriage is unsteady, and sets about arranging the two of them. Woody Allen builds the picture on that sort of household management, in a family where half-sisters, engagements and parental appetites are all discussed at the same table. A hundred and one minutes across an ensemble this size means scenes end the moment they have done their work; nobody is granted a long private crisis. What holds it together is the assurance of the very comfortable - people for whom love is a matter to be organised, and who assume the organising will go well. Europe's film academy gave it the award for the year's best film made outside Europe, a measure of how far this small stretch of Manhattan travelled.

The story arrives through a man so old that no one left alive can contradict him. Jack Crabb was raised by one people and later rode with the army against them, and Arthur Penn lets him tell it as a life rather than a case: episodes, reversals, trades, a change of clothes for each new allegiance. Two hours and nineteen minutes accommodates a great deal of swerving, and the swerving is the method - a scene played for broad comedy followed, with no warning given, by one held still while something irreparable happens. Because Crabb keeps crossing back and forth, neither the settlers nor the people who raised him can be sorted into the usual two columns. It sits in the National Film Registry. What keeps it alive is the voice: a survivor's account, unreliable by design, given by a man with nothing left to protect.

For most of its length, this account of the months before Pearl Harbor is about paperwork. Cables are decoded and mistranslated, an embargo tightens, staff officers argue over charts, and two governments move toward a war their negotiators are still formally trying to prevent. Toshio Masuda films the Japanese preparations with the same procedural evenness given to American duty rosters, so there is no room in the picture where an audience is invited to stand and cheer. Two hours and twenty-four minutes of getting ready. The suspense is administrative, accumulating out of small failures of routing and belief rather than any single blunder. The Academy's award for cinematography went to the scale of it, though the harder feat is the premise: that a catastrophe this size was assembled from ordinary competence and ordinary delay.

Bob is the difficult part: an older brother watching the younger one's love song go national from inside the same house. Luis Valdez gives him something close to equal footing with Ritchie Valens, and the film keeps returning the pair to a household where one brother's sudden earnings sit awkwardly beside the other's lack of any. Los Angeles, 1958. A ballad written for a girlfriend, an audience acquired almost overnight, a first national tour booked alongside Buddy Holly. What Valdez is careful about is the speed of it - success here is not a montage of triumph but a schedule that leaves a teenager less and less time at home. The National Film Registry took the film in later. A hundred and eight minutes, plainly shot, and patient in the scenes between brothers, which is where the accounting gets done.

The quarrel is street business before it is anything else: idle young men in a town small enough that rivals meet by accident. Franco Zeffirelli plays the first hour for that heat, staging the feud as brawling among people who inherited a grievance older than any of them, and the love story arrives inside the fighting rather than above it. The production is Italian, the verse English, and the combination alters the sound of the play; lines get hurried, thrown away, spoken while somebody is already walking off. Two hours and eighteen minutes leaves the courtship room to be awkward, which suits adolescents better than eloquence does. The Academy's award for costume design did casting work as much as decoration - the clothes sort the young men into factions, so a scuffle in a square reads at once as politics.

A short-order kitchen is a poor place to conduct anything private, which is much of the reason this romance takes nearly two hours. Johnny comes out of prison on a forgery charge into a job cooking at a New York diner, and the film keeps him there: orders called, plates up, a brief thing with one waitress complicating his interest in her friend. Garry Marshall directs a workplace picture with a courtship inside it, and the courtship advances by inches because Frankie has decided in advance that it will not. The patience is unusual. Nobody is transformed by a speech, a friend's nudging accomplishes more than any grand gesture, and refusal is allowed to be reasonable rather than coy. The National Board of Review included it in its ten for the year, which suggests how much credit the film earned for taking two tired people at their word.

Eighty-seven minutes, one outpost, two professions that cannot agree. The scientists at an arctic station and the Air Force officers posted with them want different things done with what has been found in the ice, and because the weather has closed and nobody is leaving, the argument has to be carried out in the same few rooms for the length of the film. That constraint is the design. A creature obliged to share a corridor with its investigators hardly needs to be shown, and the threat tends to arrive as information before it arrives as a body. Christian Nyby's picture sits in the National Film Registry beside far grander productions. Its method is modest and difficult to copy: frighten by watching capable people work steadily through their procedures until the procedures run out.

A fashion crew takes over a Greenwich Village bookshop, and the clerk who works there is unimpressed by all of it. That mismatch runs the length of the film: a musical about clothes and photographs whose heroine would rather be reading, carried off to Paris to be looked at and spending much of her time there arguing. Stanley Donen keeps the friction pleasant rather than sharp, though he does not pretend it away - she is a reluctant subject, and the man behind the camera is sure he is doing her a kindness. The Academy's award for costume design marks where the picture's appetite lies, and the appetite is honest: shop windows, studio light, colour used as an event, numbers staged inside the working day of a magazine. A hundred and three minutes in which neither party quite concedes the other's idea of a serious life.

The father hears the talent before anyone else does, and then he takes over the running of it. Gregory Nava's film is as much about Abraham's management as about his daughter's singing: small Texas venues, a family band whose members are also employees, a schedule set by a man certain he is protecting everyone inside it. When the guitarist becomes more than a guitarist, the trouble is less moral than administrative, a dispute within a business that happens to be a household. The other pressure is language. Selena Quintanilla sings in Spanish to Mexican-American audiences while an English-language record is prepared for a wider market, and the film is candid about the labour of belonging to two audiences at once, neither of which can be handled carelessly. The National Film Registry holds it. A hundred and twenty-seven minutes, generous with the performances.

The marriage at the centre of the film is a happy one, and that is the difficulty. Mike Leigh puts a settled couple near retirement in the middle of the frame and brings to them, across the four seasons of a single year, the friends and relatives whose lives did not settle: someone arriving early and staying late, someone with an evening to get through and then another. Their kindness is real and apparently inexhaustible, which is what makes it uncomfortable to watch being received. A hundred and twenty-nine minutes, the same rooms revisited, each visit measuring how far a guest has slipped since the last. The comedy sits very close to cruelty - a laugh at somebody's chatter arrives a beat before the recognition that she has nowhere else to take it. Europe's film academy gave its acting award to work that is the whole instrument here.

In 1949 a composer is executed for the murder of his wife; forty years later a woman who cannot speak turns up with no memory and a link to the case nobody can explain. Kenneth Branagh runs the two periods as genuinely separate worlds, cutting between the Los Angeles of the trial and the city four decades on, letting the older story keep its formal manners while the newer one does the legwork. The pleasure is in the machinery. This is a mystery designed to be assembled out of echoes and repetitions, played with the straight face such constructions require, and it makes no apology for the melodrama it runs on. A hundred and seven minutes, briskly cut, romance and investigation sharing the same scenes. The National Board of Review's ten for the year included it; the nerve is what carries it.
